---
title: "11 - Data Cleaning"
output: html_document
---

## Purpose

This file loads the raw CDC data, fixes its problems, and saves the clean data as `12_DataSaving.RData`.

## 1. Load our functions

We load our cleaning functions from `01_funct_DataCleaning.R`.

```{r load}
source("01_funct_DataCleaning.R")
```

## 2. Read the data

We read the data and check its size.

```{r read}
raw <- read.csv("data/cdc_monthly_mortality.csv")
dim(raw)
```

The data has 3,960 rows and 24 columns. Each row gives the number of deaths in one month for one group of people (by sex, race/ethnicity and age).

## 3. Rename columns

We look at a few of the column names.

```{r names_before}
colnames(raw)[c(12, 15, 22)]
```

These names are very long, so we give all columns short names.

```{r rename}
df <- rename_columns(raw)
colnames(df)
```

## 4. Change death counts to numbers

We check how R read the death count columns.

```{r counts_before}
count_cols <- colnames(df)[10:24]
str(df[, count_cols[1:4]])
```

Most of these columns are text (`chr`) instead of numbers, because numbers above 999 have commas (like `"1,355"`). We remove the commas and change these columns to numbers.

```{r counts_after}
df <- clean_counts(df, count_cols)
str(df[, count_cols[1:4]])
```

Now all of these columns are numbers (`num`).

## 5. Fix the sex column

We look at how sex is written in each year.

```{r sex_before}
table(df$sex, df$year)
```

In 2019, sex is written as `M` and `F`. In 2020 and 2021, it is written as `Male` and `Female`. We change `M` and `F` to `Male` and `Female` so all years match.

```{r sex_after}
df <- recode_sex(df)
table(df$sex, df$year)
```

Now every year uses `Female` and `Male`.

## 6. Change categories to factors

Race/ethnicity and age group are categories, so we make them factors. We make age group an ordered factor so it goes from youngest to oldest.

```{r factors}
df <- set_factors(df)
levels(df$race_ethnicity)
levels(df$age_group)
```

There are 6 race/ethnicity groups and 10 age groups, and the age groups are now in order from youngest to oldest.

## 7. Remove columns we do not need

We check the values in `analysis_date` and `jurisdiction`.

```{r constant}
table(df$analysis_date)
table(df$jurisdiction)
```

Both columns have the same value in every row, so they do not tell us anything. We also do not need `start_date` and `end_date`, because `year` and `month` already tell us when the deaths happened. We remove these four columns.

```{r drop}
df$analysis_date <- NULL
df$jurisdiction  <- NULL
df$start_date    <- NULL
df$end_date      <- NULL
dim(df)
```

The data now has 20 columns.

## 8. Remove the last few months

The CDC made this data in October 2021, so the newest months may not be complete. The `ill_defined` column counts deaths with no clear cause. We check this number for each month of 2021.

```{r ill_defined}
for (m in 1:9) {
  total <- sum(df$ill_defined[df$year == 2021 & df$month == m])
  print(paste("2021, month", m, ":", total, "ill-defined deaths"))
}
```

This number jumps after June 2021, likely because the cause of many recent deaths was not known yet. Because of this, we only keep January 2019 to June 2021.

```{r cutoff}
keep <- (df$year < 2021) | (df$month <= 6)
df <- df[keep, ]
table(df$year)
```

Now 2021 has 720 rows (6 months) instead of 1,080 (9 months).

## 9. Check the data

We count the missing values, and the rows where natural deaths are more than total deaths.

```{r checks}
sum(count_missing(df))
sum(df$natural_cause > df$all_cause)
```

Both are 0, so there are no missing values and no impossible counts. Next, we count the rows in each month.

```{r rows_per_month}
table(df$year, df$month)
```

Each month has 120 rows (2 sexes x 6 race/ethnicity groups x 10 age groups), so no month is missing or repeated. Months after June 2021 show 0 because we removed them in Step 8.

## 10. Save the clean data

We save the clean data so the next file can use it.

```{r save}
df_clean <- df
save(df_clean, file = "12_DataSaving.RData")
dim(df_clean)
```

The clean data has 3,600 rows and 20 columns. It is saved as `12_DataSaving.RData`.
